items.text: SEASON 11 · EPISODE 9 · DRAFT  The Brennock County EOC · between storms · Maya, Director Oduya, and every owner in the room · Level L6 · Mastery support (reference only — choose the tool and say why)  Two storms taught the room eleven things. The state has sent money for most of them. The last review this county ran ended in “lessons learned” — and five of those lessons are back.  ⚑ RV-182: the director owns the plan, the spending and every acceptance. RV-183: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock — and some depend on your loadout.

items.prompt: 09:10. Every owner is in the room. How does the review run?

options.result: Two findings are never mentioned — the people who'd have raised them keep quiet.

options.label: One blameless timeline of both storms, everyone adding to it; for each finding, ask what the system made easy to get wrong — then name an owner and a date
options.result: Eleven findings on one line. Three had owners before today; by lunch, eleven do.

options.label: Maya writes the review alone and circulates it
options.result: Thorough — and nobody in the room owns a word of it.

options.label: Skip the review — there's a flood season to prepare for
options.result: The flood season gets the same eleven findings.

items.title: Eleven findings, three owners.
items.body: On one timeline the two storms read like a single story: a wall on UTC, a failover that followed every flap, a mast making its own frequency, a warning rewritten, a switch that wouldn't transfer, a briefing that shut people out, hour sixteen, an open port. Before today, three of the eleven had a named owner. The other eight lived between two departments, each sure the other had it.
items.label: Test: how many gained owners — and how do you score one?

items.sub: Mastery · the skill behind this chapter

items.title: 2019 · ‘lessons learned: 14’
items.body: The county's last after-action report, from 2019: ‘Lessons learned: 14.’ No owners, no dates. Five of the fourteen are on this year's list too.

items.prompt: $250k, eleven findings, all scored. How is it spent?
items.risk: Money spent where it's seen, not where it's needed.
timeout: The money waits; the flood season doesn't.

hints.text: Which findings fail worst and most often?

options.label: Split it evenly across the departments
options.result: Everyone gets something; the conduit and the transfer switch get a fraction each.
options.consequence: Fair to departments, not to risk.

options.label: By risk, with the owners: the separate path and backup power first, then handovers, the gateway, templates, ports, patch tests and failback — $216k for 140 of 143 points; the wall and chairs unfunded
options.result: Oduya reads the ranking twice: “I can defend every line of this.”
options.consequence: Money where the risk is — explained in numbers the director can defend.

options.label: The second video wall — it's what people see
options.result: A beautiful wall over the same conduit.
options.consequence: Buys the most visible thing, not the most important.

options.label: Save it for the rebuild
options.result: The next storm arrives before the rebuild.
options.consequence: Leaves every known risk open for a year.

items.title: The city that raised itself
items.body: In September 1900 a hurricane's storm surge swept over Galveston, Texas, and killed thousands of people. The city's answer was not a report. It built a seawall along the Gulf, and then — house by house, street by street — raised the ground of the whole city by several feet, pumping sand in beneath buildings jacked up on screws. An after-action review is only as good as what gets built because of it.

items.title: The risk we're choosing.
items.body: The tranche retires almost all of the scored risk. Not all. The second wall and the new chairs are left over — and one finding is bigger than any tranche: the room itself. Too small for six agencies at full activation, its wall controller at end of life, one conduit from a dark room. The state's full rebuild grant closes at 08:00 on the 14th. The forecast puts the next crest on the 13th.
items.label: Test: what's spent — and who signs for what isn't?

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #110 · AVERY'S LENS  An after-action ends in owners, dates and signatures  A review that ends in lessons changes nothing. Every finding needs an owner and a date; the money goes where the risk is worst; whatever isn't funded is accepted, in writing, by the person who owns it.  Eight of eleven findings from two storms had no owner — and the money could fix most of the risk, not all of it.

items.alt: The EOC; Director Oduya holds a pen over the risk register; Maya beside her with the ranked plan.

bubbles.text: Why should I put my name on accepting a risk? That's how directors get blamed.
It's already your risk. Signing it makes it a decision instead of an accident.

options.label: “Nobody reads the register.”
options.reply: Then why am I signing it?

items.prompt: What happens to the risk the tranche can't buy?
items.risk: Accepted risks nobody remembers accepting — and a rebuild that misses its deadline.
timeout: The leftovers are forgotten by spring.

hints.text: What turns a leftover into a decision?

items.note: Draft decision (DR-S11E09). Option B needs Documentation at LIMITED or better.

options.label: Leave it off the plan — nobody needs reminding
options.result: Next year nobody remembers it was a choice.

options.label: The unfunded items go on the county's risk register with an owner, a review date and the director's signed acceptance; the room rebuild goes into the state's full grant application, owned by the director
options.result: Oduya signs: ‘Second wall and chairs — accepted until next year.’ The rebuild application has her name on the cover and Maya's design inside.
options.consequence: Chosen risk, signed; the big finding given its own path.

options.label: List the unfunded items in an email to the director
options.result: She reads it. Nobody can find it in March.
options.consequence: The best you can do without a register — known, not recorded.

options.label: Fund the chairs by cutting the patch tests

items.alt: The after-action sheet as signed: every one of the eleven findings with an owner; eight marked funded, the update window fixed in the first week; the second wall and chairs marked ‘accepted · signed’. $216k retires 140 of the 143 risk points still open; the rest accepted by the director in writing.
items.caption: A decision instead of an accident.

items.title: rebuild · ‘closes 08:00, the 14th’
items.body: The state's notice for the full rebuild grant: ‘Applications close 08:00 on the 14th. Include a needs analysis, a scoped design and a five-year cost.’ The long-range forecast puts the next crest on the 13th.

items.alt: The EOC on Friday afternoon; Director Oduya holds the signed plan; Hektor holds the retest report for the transfer switch.

bubbles.text: Eleven names. Eleven dates. One signature — mine.
And the switch retested, on the first Friday. Ten seconds.

items.alt: The Sable River at night, far over its banks, rain driving; the road under water; Maya by her car with her phone.

bubbles.text: The Sable's going to a record crest by eight tomorrow. Carrier A is down again. And someone's posting that the dam's gone. I need you in the room.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  An after-action review ends in owners, dates and signatures, not lessons. One blameless timeline; an owner and a date for every finding; money spent by risk (R = L × I) and explained in numbers; whatever isn’t funded goes on the register with the owner’s signed acceptance — a decision instead of an accident. And when a finding is bigger than the money, give it its own path and its own owner.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Which of your “lessons learned” has come back a second time?
